doc.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Switching to trombone, Rocks McConnell, and Hingham ammunition depot
summary: He moves from tuba to trombone, covers for a deserter trombonist, is sent to Hingham, Massachusetts, and jams in Boston with Sabby Lewis.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: About what year would this have been when you changed over from the trombone to the tuba?
From the tuba to the trombone?

Yes, from the tuba to the trombone, was in 19 — I went into the Navy in 1942, so this was like 1939. And so I wanted to play in the band because they had all these great musicians: Clark Terry and Osie Johnson and Dudley Brooks and all these famous musicians, but they wouldn’t let me in because they were using the string bass now. And so I would get up and go into the head in the morning and start practicing on the trombone because it was a bass clef instrument, and finally, one of the guys went over the hill one day, which was Rocks McConnell, who was one of the all-time great trombone players at that time, and he wrote a tune called “Sweet Slumber,” which he played with Lucky Millender’s great orchestra, and this tune had become a hit, and here he was in the service, and a big check came to him and he went over the hill, and I have never seen him since — none of us — he just disappeared. So here Al Grey comes along to sit in for him for inspection, where they come through and inspect all your clothes etcetera, and the band, and I would sit in his chair to cover for him, which we hoped that he would come back. And from this, this is where I got teaching from many of the great artists that was in the band, and they then sent me out to New England, out there in Hingham, Massachusetts, which was an ammunition depot, where they had so many people in the Navy that could not read or write at that time. And I used to even write letters home to some of the kids’ parents and everything like that. Because when they would go get paid they would make this X. See now you’re not going to hear none of this kind of talk today, because it’s not like that anymore. But at that time it was. And we had the freedom of going out anywhere we wished, as a musician, see? Because all we did was play music. Now they did all of this stevedore work in the igloos and things where they had smokeless powder and all like this, but we played in the band. And what happened to me is that I would go into Boston, and go jamming with Sabby Lewis, who had a famous band, and this is where I learned more about playing jazz, because he had a great, great group.
